sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Proton Therapy vs SBRT: Which Is Right for You?
sectionToMerge.intro: Proton therapy and SBRT are two advanced radiation techniques, and the right choice depends on your cancer type, tumour location, stage, and treatment goals. These FAQs explain how each works, who they may suit, and how international patients can access them.

items.a: Proton therapy is a type of radiation treatment that uses charged particles called protons instead of conventional X-rays to destroy cancer cells. Protons release most of their energy at a precise depth and then stop, which can reduce the radiation dose to surrounding healthy tissue. It may be considered for tumours near sensitive organs or in children, though suitability depends on cancer type, location, stage, and specialist review.

items.q: What is SBRT (stereotactic body radiation therapy)?
items.a: SBRT is a highly focused form of radiation that delivers very high doses to a small tumour over a few sessions. It uses advanced imaging and precise targeting to shape the beams tightly around the tumour while limiting exposure to nearby tissue. SBRT may be suitable for selected small, well-defined tumours in the lung, liver, spine, or prostate, but the treating radiation oncology team decides based on each case.

items.q: What is the main difference between proton therapy and SBRT?
items.a: The main difference is the type of radiation used and how the dose is delivered. Proton therapy uses proton particles that stop at a set depth, potentially sparing tissue beyond the tumour, while SBRT uses focused X-ray beams delivered in a few high-dose sessions. Both aim for precision, but the better fit depends on tumour type, size, location, and overall health, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: Which is better, proton therapy or SBRT?
items.a: Neither proton therapy nor SBRT is universally better, as each has advantages for different situations. Proton therapy may help when nearby healthy organs must be protected, while SBRT is often effective for small, clearly defined tumours treated in a short course. The right option depends on cancer type, stage, tumour location, previous treatment, and specialist review, and final decisions should be made by the treating medical team.

items.q: Who is a good candidate for proton therapy?
items.a: Proton therapy may be suitable for selected patients whose tumours sit close to critical structures, such as the brain, spine, eyes, or heart, and for many children where reducing radiation to growing tissue matters. It may also be considered for certain head, neck, and prostate cancers. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, tumour location, previous treatment, and overall health, and should be confirmed by a radiation oncology team after review.

items.q: Who is a good candidate for SBRT?
items.a: SBRT may be considered for patients with small, well-defined tumours that can be targeted precisely, such as early-stage lung cancer, some liver tumours, spinal lesions, and localised prostate cancer. It is often chosen when a patient cannot have surgery or prefers a shorter treatment course. Suitability depends on tumour size, location, number of lesions, and overall health, and final decisions should be made by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What are the side effects of proton therapy versus SBRT?
items.a: Both proton therapy and SBRT can cause side effects, though these vary by treatment site and dose. Common effects may include fatigue, skin changes, and irritation of nearby organs, such as cough or breathlessness for lung treatment. Because both techniques are precise, they aim to limit damage to healthy tissue, but no treatment is risk-free. Possible side effects should be discussed in detail with the treating radiation oncology team.

items.q: How many treatment sessions does each require?
items.a: The number of sessions differs between the two approaches and depends on the individual plan. SBRT is usually delivered in a small number of sessions, often between one and five, because each dose is high and focused. Proton therapy is more often given as a longer course over several weeks, similar to conventional radiotherapy. The exact schedule depends on cancer type, tumour location, and the treating team's assessment.

items.q: How much does proton therapy cost compared to SBRT?
items.a: Proton therapy is generally more expensive than SBRT because it requires specialised equipment and facilities that are less widely available. Exact costs cannot be fixed in advance, as they depend on the hospital, country, cancer type, number of sessions, additional tests, and length of stay. SBRT is often more affordable due to shorter courses and wider availability. Final costs should be confirmed with the treating hospital based on your diagnosis.

items.q: Is proton therapy available in India?
items.a: Proton therapy is available at a limited number of specialised centres in India, while SBRT is offered more widely across major cancer hospitals. Access depends on the specific centre, waiting times, and whether the technique suits your cancer type and stage. Availability and suitability should be confirmed directly with the hospital after a medical review, and final treatment decisions rest with the qualified oncology team managing your care.

items.q: Which countries offer proton therapy and SBRT?
items.a: SBRT is available in many countries with modern radiotherapy departments, while proton therapy is offered in fewer locations, including centres in the United States, several European countries, Japan, China, and parts of India. Access depends on hospital availability, capacity, and whether the treatment matches your diagnosis. International patients should confirm availability and suitability with each centre, as acceptance depends on medical review and the treating team's assessment.

items.q: Are there clinical trials comparing proton therapy and SBRT?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials are studying proton therapy and SBRT for various cancers, sometimes comparing them directly to understand which offers better outcomes or fewer side effects. Participation does not guarantee benefit or enrolment, as trials have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment. Patients interested in trials should discuss suitable options with their oncology team and the trial investigators.

items.q: Can proton therapy and SBRT be combined with other treatments?
items.a: Both proton therapy and SBRT may be combined with other treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, depending on the cancer type and stage. Radiation may be used before or after other treatments as part of an overall plan. Whether combining treatments is appropriate depends on your diagnosis, previous therapy, and overall health, and should be planned and coordinated by a multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: Is proton therapy or SBRT better for recurrent cancer?
items.a: For recurrent cancer, the choice between proton therapy and SBRT depends on where the tumour has returned and how much radiation the area received before. Proton therapy may help limit dose to previously treated tissue, while SBRT can precisely target small recurrent tumours. Re-treatment carries added risks and requires careful evaluation. The safest option depends on prior treatment, tumour location, and overall health, and must be decided by the treating team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to decide between proton therapy and SBRT?
items.a: Deciding between proton therapy and SBRT usually requires recent imaging such as CT, MRI, or PET scans, along with pathology or biopsy reports, staging details, and a summary of previous treatments. These records help the radiation oncology team assess tumour size, location, and suitability for each technique. A second opinion may also be helpful. Gathering complete and up-to-date reports supports a faster and more accurate treatment recommendation.

items.q: Can international patients travel abroad for proton therapy or SBRT?
items.a: International patients can travel abroad for proton therapy or SBRT, but access is not guaranteed and depends on several factors. These include hospital acceptance after medical review, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's overall condition. Because proton centres are fewer, planning ahead is important. Patients should arrange medical reports, a treatment estimate, and travel details in advance, understanding that admission and treatment acceptance remain at the hospital's discretion.

items.q: How long will I need to stay for treatment?
items.a: The length of stay depends on which treatment you receive and your recovery needs. SBRT often requires a shorter stay because it is delivered in only a few sessions, while proton therapy may need several weeks due to its longer course. Additional time may be needed for assessments, planning scans, and follow-up. The treating team can give a more accurate estimate once your treatment plan and schedule are confirmed.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with proton therapy vs SBRT?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support aims to make comparing proton therapy and SBRT clearer, without replacing the guidance of the treating doctors and hospital.
